courses.description: This course is integrated with global citizenship instruction and utilizes cultural exploration as a way to develop skills in thematic development, character analysis, research analysis, inferential thinking and writing towards a specific audience and purpose. Reading will cover a variety of genres, including both fiction and nonfiction. Students work independently and collaboratively through a variety of mediums and formats to gain exposure and aptitude with informative, narrative, and argumentative writing. Students gain the opportunity to collaborate with peers in small and whole group discussions in order to develop a further understanding of content specific skills.

In this course of study, students will examine both world and ‘closer to home’ issues through reading, research, analyzing the perspectives of authors, and create an understanding of those issues through writing in a variety of contexts. This class is writing intensive, and students will be able to refine their writing skills in the areas of argument, narrative, and explanatory writing. Students will be asked to study pieces of literature, as well as shorter texts, in the context of when they were written, and compare this context with the current cultural context of the region. Assessment is accomplished through discussion, small group activities and written responses such as journals, creative writing and formal essays.

Communication is an essential component of success in nearly every aspect of life. In this course, you will learn to use reading, writing, speaking, and listening in to address specific, real-world challenges you will face as an adult. You will refine your media literacy skills, learning how to evaluate the reliability of online information through source analysis and corroboration. You will become a more informed consumer by gaining an understanding of the advertising and propaganda strategies that companies and politicians use to persuade you to buy their products or vote for them. You will develop your own argumentation skills by researching and writing about a controversial topic of your choice and engaging in debates. Finally, you become an informed citizen by learning how communities work together and how you can participate in government and the electoral process.

The ability to communicate verbally in a wide variety of settings, both formal and informal, is a critically important skill not only in college but also in your career and personal life. In this course, you will learn how to engage your audience while developing confidence in your public speaking ability. You will prepare and deliver various types of presentations to inform, persuade, and entertain. You will also learn how to give and receive feedback, talk constructively about controversial issues, and detect when a speaker is trying to manipulate you through false logic. Though public speaking is something many students fear, you CAN improve and learn how to do it effectively - it just takes practice!
courses.notes: College level available (dual enrollment): Meet with Guidance to complete the necessary paperwork for Dual Enrollment.

courses.description: Seeing the world through another’s eyes broadens your perspective on others and on yourself. Contemporary World Literature introduces students to the stories of a wide variety of people throughout the world. Through both fiction and non-fiction, we will explore the range of human experience across national and cultural boundaries, seeking both cultural differences and the broad similarities that make us all human. This class may be taken either as a dual enrollment course through the Community College of Vermont or as a regular high school course, however significant amounts of reading and writing, including frequent homework, will be expected of all students.
courses.notes: College option available (dual enrollment): Meet with Guidance to complete the necessary paperwork for Dual Enrollment

courses.description: Why do people argue about immigration? How does a presidential campaign work? How do I know what news sources to trust? Investigate the answers to these questions and many more as we learn about some of the major issues facing the United States and the world today. Students will research the history of current conflicts, debate controversial topics, and learn how to evaluate evidence and perspective on multiple sides of complex issues.
courses.notes: Also listed under Global Citizenship (p. 19)

courses.description: “The past is never dead. It isn’t even past.” William Faulkner, one of the most famous writers from the American South, could have been talking about the Civil War when he made this statement. The Civil War was the most traumatic event in American history. It literally ripped the national apart; brothers fought brothers, friends fought friends, and more Americans died than in any other war in history. We will examine why the war happened, how it affected both soldiers and civilians, and how its legacy continues to affect us even now, over 150 years after the last shot was fired.
courses.offering_note: This class is offered every other year. The next time it will be offered is: 2025-2026 (stale date as printed in 2026-27 catalog)
courses.notes: Also listed under Global Citizenship (p. 19)

courses.description: Tanks. Airplanes. Machine guns. World War I is often called the first modern war, as it saw the first widespread use of industrial-age military technology. By 1918, 15 million soldiers and civilians had died; people labeled it “The War to End All Wars” and swore that it would never happen again. But it did. By 1939, the world was once again at war, in an even more destructive conflict that included the horrors of the Holocaust and the atomic bomb. Through an examination of primary and secondary historical sources, literature, film, and art, we will analyze why these wars happened, how they impacted people on all sides of the conflicts, and how they created the world we know today.
courses.offering_note: This class is offered every other year. The next time it will be offered is: 2027-2028
courses.notes: Also listed under Global Citizenship (p. 19)

courses.description: The focus of this class is to prepare students for literacy success after high school. Units of study may include informational writing units heavily focused on career exploration and entrepreneurship, as well as instructional writing and argumentative writing units. Students will have the opportunity for hands-on learning in order to influence their understanding of the application of English in real world situations.

How does our culture impact our daily lives? How do our beliefs shape our lives? How can we affect change in our society? These are some of the guiding questions in a course which is integrated with ELA instruction and utilizes exposure to a variety of cultures as a way to develop knowledge in historical context and perspectives. Students will explore such topics as immigration, religion, natural disasters, social movements, and governmental systems through the use of primary and secondary sources. This course will culminate in a ‘World’s Fair’ in which students will examine global customs and cuisines from a variety of global countries and cultures.

What are the rights and responsibilities of a citizen? This is the driving question we explore in Civics. In Civics we will look at local, state, and federal government, how each are set up and how decisions are made at each level. We will explore the election process and learn the role of elected and appointed officials in each level of the government. Immigration and citizenship will also be explored as we look at the rights and responsibilities an individual has as a U.S. citizen and the processes by which someone becomes a citizen of the United States of America. In Criminal and Civil Law we will explore the U.S. judicial system and how the criminal and civil legal systems work. Civil law will explore the areas of private rights and remedies and deal with issues such as contracts, property, and family law. Criminal law looks at the criminal justice system and how criminal acts of violent and property crimes are addressed.

An introduction to psychological terms, facts and principles designed to aid the student in understanding individual behavior. Behavior is analyzed and interpreted through activities and discussions of such topics as motivation, emotion, perception, learning, and intelligence. This course may be offered for dual enrollment credit.
courses.notes: College option available (dual enrollment): Meet with Guidance to complete the necessary paperwork for Dual Enrollment.

courses.description: In History and Music, we will explore different time periods starting with ancient Greece and ending with modern times. We will study the music and historical events in those eras. This class can be taken for either a Global Citizenship or Fine Art credit.
courses.fulfills_text: This class can be taken for either a Global Citizenship or Fine Art credit.
courses.notes: Also listed under Fine Arts (p. 32)

courses.description: Reel History is an opportunity to examine, consider, discuss, and debate America’s past as portrayed through Hollywood’s lens. We’ll look at a range of films to discover what stories are told, by whom, with what degree of accuracy, and why.

Integrated Math 1 is designed to engage all students with opportunities to explore data, patterns, shape, and change in realistic contexts and situations. Students will develop an understanding of algebraic, geometric and statistical reasoning through a problem solving approach. Each unit focuses on the overarching theme that patterns are the foundation of mathematics and that these patterns can be communicated through multiple representations. Math 1 is designed to capitalize on students’ strengths and intuition to build capacity for deeper mathematical understanding.

In this course, students will deepen their understanding of key mathematical concepts across algebra, geometry, functions, and statistics. They will work with linear, quadratic, and exponential functions through multiple representations and apply these models to real-world problems. Students will explore surface area, volume, similarity, dilations, the Pythagorean Theorem, and right triangle trigonometry to analyze spatial relationships. They will also build reasoning skills by constructing proofs involving geometric figures and by examining statistical inference and study design. Through problem solving, modeling, and collaborative learning, students will see how mathematical ideas connect across topics and real-world contexts.

This course will cover the following Common Core math standards: Number and Quantity: rational exponents; perform arithmetic operations with complex numbers; use complex numbers in polynomial identities and equations. Algebra: seeing structure in expressions; relationship between zeros and factors; use polynomial identities to solve problems; rewriting rational expressions; create and solve equations and inequalities in one variable; solve systems of equations; represent equations and inequalities graphically. Modeling with Functions: understand the concept of a function and use function notation; interpret, analyze and construct functions that arise in various applications or which model a relationship between two quantities; construct and compare linear, quadratic and exponential functions. Inferences and Conclusions from Data: make inferences and justify conclusions from sample surveys, experiments and observational studies; use probability to evaluate outcomes of decisions.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Algebra I and Geometry

courses.description: This course will cover the following Common Core math standards: Number and Quantity: represent complex numbers and their operations on the complex plane; evaluating roots and radicals of complex numbers; extend complex numbers to fractal equations; represent and model with vector quantities; perform operations on vectors. Trigonometric Functions: analyze functions using different representations with a concentration on trigonometric functions; extend the domain of trigonometric functions using the unit circle; application to surveying problems (earth distance problems, property area calculations); prove and apply trigonometric identities; model periodic phenomena with trigonometric functions.
courses.notes: College level available (dual enrollment): Meet with Guidance to complete the necessary paperwork for Dual Enrollment.

courses.description: Introduction to Data Science (IDS) is designed to introduce students to the exciting opportunities available at the intersection of data analysis, computing and mathematics through hands-on activities. Data are everywhere, and this class will help prepare students to live in a world of data. The class focuses on practical application of data analysis to give students concrete and applicable skills. Instead of using small, tailored, curated data sets as in a traditional statistics curriculum, this class engages students with a wider world of data that fall into the "Big Data" paradigm and are relevant to students' lives. In IDS statistical inference is taught algorithmically, using modern randomization and simulation techniques. Students will learn to find and communicate meaning in data, and to think critically about arguments based on data.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Algebra 2 OR concurrent enrollment in Algebra 2

courses.description: Embark on a delectable journey with our Culinary Arts and Business Math course, where the art of baking meets the principles of entrepreneurship. In this comprehensive high school program, students will master the essential techniques of baking, from bread to pastries, while concurrently developing proficiency in business math. The course seamlessly integrates hands-on baking experiences with practical applications of budgeting, pricing strategies, profit and loss calculations, and inventory management. Through collaborative projects and real-world simulations, students will not only refine their culinary skills but also cultivate a foundational understanding of the mathematics crucial for success in the culinary and business realms
courses.notes: Also listed under Practical Arts (p. 29)

courses.description: This Science Technology Engineering and Mathematics (STEM) course provides a holistic approach to the sciences through an engineering lens. This course aims to provide students with a baseline understanding of the core disciplines of science. Chemistry, physics, biology, and Earth science are integrated in students’ freshman year. Topics of study are grounded in Earth Science. These topics include weather and climate, plate tectonics, weathering and erosion, alternative energy, and our impact on the Earth. Curriculum for this course is based on the Next Generation Science Standards (NGSS).

This course investigates the study of living things. Through classroom discussions, experimentation, and modeling, students become familiar with some of the unifying principles governing living things, and why citizens need to know biology to make informed personal decisions. Diverse units of study include ecosystems: interactions, energy, and dynamics, molecules to organisms: structure and processes, heredity: inheritance and variation of traits, and biological evolution: unity and diversity. Students will be engaged in asking questions such as why viruses and bacteria are often difficult to control, why reliance on antibiotics has resulted in resistant strains of bacteria will be studied, how human activities in the watershed impact the health of Lake Champlain, and how the health of the organism is dependent on the health of the body cells. The PBGR’s assessed in this course include transferable skills (citizenship, collaboration), content standards (scientific analysis and interpretation, scientific communication, science experimental design, and scientific modeling, science explanation and argument).

courses.course_name: Honors PLTW: Principles of Biomedical Science
courses.description: From design and data analysis to outbreaks, clinical empathy, health promotion, and more, students explore the vast range of careers in biomedical sciences. They develop not just technical skills, but also in-demand, transportable skills that they need to thrive in life and career.

Students experience real-world scenarios and mock cases to see medicine in action – as they learn through projects, lab investigations, and case studies to diagnose and provide treatment and rehabilitation to patients at an outpatient center, keep clients safe and healthy on adventure medicine trips in remote locations, and work in a research center to design laboratory investigations to explore development and aging.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Principles of Biomedical Science
courses.offering_note: The next time it will be offered is: 2027-2028

courses.description: This class is a mathematics based science class in which students will study the fundamentals of Chemistry including but not limited to the following: The periodic table of elements, atoms, isotopes, chemical naming, bonding and structure, mole calculations, stoichiometry, balancing equations, types of reactions, solubility and acid-base theory.
courses.prerequisites: successful completion of Algebra I with skills including algebraic manipulation, basic graphing and math computation.

courses.description: This class is computer based, lab intensive, where students will learn, design, and conduct investigations into the fundamentals of physics. Topics included but are not limited to: interactions of matter and energy, distance, displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, energy, momentum and charge. Students will be challenged to apply their knowledge of the laws of physics to solve physics related critical thinking problems.

This course is designed to provide students with an opportunity to engage in various science domains and science inquiry, as they apply the skills and knowledge to crime scene investigation. Students will learn forensic techniques, evidence collection, data collection, and analysis and explanation as applied to case studies. Course strands include trace evidence, fingerprints, DNA, blood, toxicology, handwriting analysis, and more. PBGR’s assessed in this course include transferable skills (citizenship, collaboration), content standards (scientific communication, science experimental design,and science explanation and argument).

The Agriculture Science class aims to analyze Vermont’s agriculture from a scientific lens. The course is project-based. Students will choose a relevant topic of interest and examine that topic through various lenses. The project is centered around the essential question: How does the landscape of Vermont influence its farmers? The course will begin with a survey of the top commodities produced in the state, and then move on to soil science, the genetics of selective breeding, and landscape ecology. This course will be offered all afternoon during one semester, and will provide a Science and English credit.
courses.fulfills_text: will provide a Science and English credit

courses.description: Build on your foundational understanding of Agriculture! We will dive deeper into topics covered in Ag. Science 1, including specific practices within our local dairy and maple industry. There will be opportunities for individual projects that include in person experiences on site, as well as shadowing and interview based exploration.

This course examines the physical, chemical, and biological processes of rivers and streams. Topics include stream features, geology, water chemistry, and human impacts relevant to river ecology. Participants will explore current issues and topics affecting watersheds and river systems from local to global. Students will engage in authentic research, design lab investigations, monitor streams, collect and analyze data, and conclude on their findings. Students will develop and carry out a stewardship project using project-based learning strategies. During the projects they will design solutions to stream problems, and take action on their scientific findings as they work to improve the local watershed with their work.

This course is an introduction to the French language. Key topics include vocabulary acquisition, verb conjugation, grammar, and idiomatic expressions. As we explore the Francophone world, we will also cover culture, geography, cultural influences, and practical implications of the language relevant to student life. The text is Bienvenue. Students will work in and out of the text, in workbooks, and with realia, film, and auditory materials. Individual and interactive group work are cornerstones of this course. Speaking, listening, reading, and writing skills are all emphasized.

It is expected that students enrolling in the class completed French I with a minimum average of a 70. This class begins where French I left off, and it is assumed that students will make an attempt to keep their skills honed in the time between French I and French II. French II focuses on more advanced grammar structures, varied verb tense usage, and integration of new words and expressions into the student’s existing French vocabulary. Conversations and Compositions will get progressively longer as students master more advanced concepts and combinations. As we continue to explore the Francophone world, we will cover new information and concepts in culture, geography, cultural influences, and practical implications of the language relevant to student life The text continues to be Bienvenue, with a possibility of moving into Aboard after the completion of the first text. Students will continue to work in and out of the text, in workbooks, and with realia, film and auditory materials. Individual and interactive group continue as cornerstones of this course. Speaking, listening, reading, and writing skills are all emphasized, though with higher production expectations than French I.

It is expected that students enrolling in this class completed French II with a minimum average of an 80. This class begins where French II or French III left off, and it is assumed that students will make an attempt to continue their skills between one class and the next. French III/IV focuses on more advanced grammar structures, usage of multiple verb tenses, and integration and spontaneous implementation of new words and expressions into the student’s existing French vocabulary. Conversations, reading assignments, and compositions will get progressively longer and more complex as students master more advanced concepts and combinations. As we continue to explore the Francophone world, we will cover new information and concepts in culture, geography, cultural influences, and practical implications of the language relevant to student life. The text is Aboard, with breaks to work in selected novels. Students will continue to work in and out of the text, in workbooks, and with realia, film and auditory materials. Individual and interactive groups continue as cornerstones of this course. Speaking, listening, reading and writing skills are all emphasized, especially in spontaneous or self-directed settings. Speaking is a very prominent focus of this course as is written and oral creative self-expression in the target language.
courses.notes: Note: Students pursuing 4 years of foreign language study may enroll in this class twice.

courses.description: This course is an introduction to the Spanish language. Key topics include vocabulary acquisition, verb conjugation, grammar, and idiomatic expressions. As we explore the Spanish-speaking world, we will also cover culture, geography, cultural influences, and practical implications of the language relevant to student life. Individual and interactive group work are cornerstones of this course. Speaking, listening, reading, and writing skills are all emphasized.

It is expected that students enrolling in the class completed Spanish I with a minimum average of a 70. This class begins where Spanish I left off, and it is assumed that students will make an attempt to keep their skills honed in the time between Spanish I and Spanish II. Spanish II focuses on more advanced grammar structures, varied verb tense usage, and integration of new words and expressions into the student’s existing Spanish vocabulary. Conversations and Compositions will get progressively longer as students master more advanced concepts and combinations. As we continue to explore the Hispanic world, we will cover new information and concepts in culture, geography, cultural influences, and practical implications of the language relevant to student life. Individual and interactive groups continue as cornerstones of this course. Speaking, listening, reading, and writing skills are all emphasized, though with higher production expectations than Spanish I.

It is expected that students enrolling in the class completed Spanish II with a minimum average of an 80. This class begins where Spanish II or left off, and it is assumed that students will make an attempt to keep their skills honed in the time between one class and the next. Spanish III focuses on more advanced grammar structures, usage of multiple verb tenses, and integration and spontaneous implementation of new words and expressions into the student’s existing Spanish vocabulary. Conversations, readings assignments, and compositions will get progressively longer and more complex as students master more advanced concepts and combinations. As we continue to explore the Hispanic world, we will cover new information and concepts in culture, geography, cultural influences, and practical implications of the language relevant to student life. Individual and interactive group continue as cornerstones of this course. Speaking, listening, reading, and writing skills are all emphasized, especially in spontaneous or self-directed settings. Speaking is a very prominent focus of this course as is written and oral creative self-expression in the target language.
courses.notes: Note: Students pursuing 4 years of foreign language study may enroll in this class twice.

courses.description: In Computer Science Essentials, students will use visual, block-based programming and seamlessly transition to text-based programming with languages such as Python® to create apps and develop websites, and learn how to make computers work together to put their design into practice. They’ll apply computational thinking practices, build their vocabulary, and collaborate just as computing professionals do to create products that address topics and problems important to them.

Using Python® as a primary tool, students learn the fundamentals of coding, data processing, data security, and task automation, while learning to contribute to an inclusive, safe, and ethical computing culture. The course promotes computational thinking and coding fundamentals and introduces computational tools that foster creativity. Computer Science Principles helps students develop programming expertise and explore the workings of the Internet. Projects and problems include app development, visualization of data, cybersecurity, and simulation. PLTW is recognized by the College Board as an endorsed provider of curriculum and professional development for AP® Computer Science Principles (AP CSP). This endorsement affirms that all components of PLTW CSP’s offerings are aligned to the AP Curriculum Framework standards and the AP CSP assessment.
courses.prerequisites: It is preferred that students will have already taken Computer Science Essentials before taking Computer Science Principles.

courses.description: Engineers make a world of difference! Students are introduced to the engineering design process, applying math, science, and engineering standards to identify and design solutions to a variety of real problems. They work both individually and in collaborative teams to develop and document design solutions using engineering notebooks and 3D modeling software. Are you ready to design the future?

Open doors to understanding electronics and foundations in circuit design. Digital electronics is the foundation of all modern electronic devices such as cellular phones, MP3 players, laptop computers, digital cameras, high definition televisions, etc. Students learn the digital circuit design process to create circuits and present solutions that can improve people’s lives. Learn how advancements in foundational electronic components and digital circuit design processes have transformed the world around you
courses.prerequisites: It is preferred that students will have already taken Intro to Engineering Essentials before taking Digital Electronics

courses.description: This course provides students with an introduction to game design and development using Unity, a game engine. Students will learn fundamental programming concepts with C#, develop interactive gameplay mechanics, and create 2D and 3D game environments. Students will design and build their own playable games, gaining experience in problem-solving, iterative design, and game development. By the end of the course, students will have a portfolio-ready game and a strong foundation for further studies or careers in game development. No prior coding experience is required.

The purpose of this course is to provide students with opportunities to develop and enhance critical life management skills necessary to make sound decisions and take positive action for healthy and effective living. Topics include: positive emotional development, nutrition, substance abuse and misuse, responsible decision making and planning, communication, coping skills, forming positive relationships, and how to avoid high-risk behaviors.

This course offers instruction in the skills, strategies, and playing of team sports without losing sight of the importance of physical fitness. The concepts of cooperation, teamwork, and sportsmanship are stressed. Depending on student interest, other types of PE can be incorporated, such as: Yoga and Pilates, Lifetime Fitness, and Strength and Conditioning.
This class will focus on different methods of wellness like yoga, Pilates, meditation, walking, and stretching.

The goal of this course is to gain a better understanding of how food and nutrition affects our bodies and lifestyles. Topics of study include food safety and sanitation, kitchen safety, nutrition, lab procedures, and preparation techniques of meats, yeast breads, sandwiches, pizza, poultry, biscuits, and dairy. This course is made up of hands-on experiences and research projects. This class can be taken twice.

This introductory hands-on sewing class emphasizes basic sewing skills such as measuring and cutting fabric, sewing buttons, and learning to use a sewing machine. Students will explore the history of quilting/sewing and create many projects using voice and choice opportunities.

Independent Study is offered to provide individual students with the opportunity to explore special talents or interests within the areas of Family and Consumer Sciences. Students will work with the classroom teacher to set personal learning goals and to determine the type of project or learning experience they would like to pursue.
courses.notes: program

courses.description: At the start of each Project; you will be presented with a design problem that I have created to teach you about the key ideas in Design Technology. Each project is designed to teach you about the following in an authentic, hands on learning experience in woodwork and metalwork.You will learn about: ● Technology in manufacturing ● Production systems (CAD/CAM) ● Product Sustainability and Social Issues ● Materials and their characteristics ● The theory of design and how to apply this to design and make creative, functional and aesthetic products that are suitable for the end user/target marketEach project encompasses real-world problems that are driven by inquiry and creative thinking, each project is largely driven by your personal hobbies and interests. You will complete each Project by following a 'Design Cycle' that has been divided into 6 stages of formal assessment. Please click on the links above to find your class, projects, and assignments.

This course will introduce students to the process of starting and maintaining a small manufacturing business. Students will develop product prototypes, select a product for mass production, work on marketing and sales, as well as conduct professional communications and manage inventory, supplies, expenses and profits. All while working within an authentic time table. This course would be taking place over multiple class periods during the day and having 2 embedded credits that fulfill both core and elective requirements. The embedded credits will be: Computer Technology and Practical Art
courses.fulfills_text: 2 embedded credits that fulfill both core and elective requirements. The embedded credits will be: Computer Technology and Practical Art

courses.description: In this class you will learn about the following art mediums: ● Drawing Learn to create 2 dimensional art and shading by practicing different techniques and mediums using graphite and different drawing utensils. ● Painting Use paint and various surfaces like canvas, paper, masonite, wood, etc to create different 2D artwork of all shapes and sizes. ● Sculpture Create 3 dimensional art by practicing different techniques and mediums over the course of the semester. Clay, carvings, plaster casting popsicle stick structures, etc Use your imagination and pitch an idea. Project based. Set daily goals based on the standards and interests.

The yearbook class allows students the opportunity to participate in the making of a real life publication. This experience develops organization, collaboration, proofreading, writing skills and meeting deadlines. Computer and typing skills are also developed. Since this is an important book, both to the school and the community, the teacher reserves the right to hand pick students who best meet these criteria.

Students are expected to take band for the entire year. Exceptions must be approved by the music instructor. Students will learn to play music of different styles and historical eras. Further development of each student’s musicianship is stressed through increasing knowledge of music fundamentals and ensemble skills. Students have the opportunity to participate in District and All State Music Festivals. Assessment is done through evaluation of daily participation, successful participation in required performances and periodic quizzes.
courses.prerequisites: One year of instrumental music study or by permission of music instructor

courses.description: Do you love to sing? Do you want to sing a variety of music with others? Are you interested in singing, but don’t know where to start? If you said “yes” to any of those questions, this may be the class for you. Students in chorus will learn the fundamentals of vocal and ensemble techniques, singing music in a variety of styles from a variety of times and places, performing a concert at the end of the semester. Students who are interested may also participate in the Northwest District Music Festival Choir (MS and HS) and the All State Music Festival (HS only). This class may be repeated.

Discover the piano! Students who take this course will learn the fundamentals of playing piano and reading music in two clefs. From scales and arpeggios to solos and duets, we will explore a variety of piano repertoire, working towards a recital at the end of the semester. Advanced piano students may also work towards accompanying the chorus or playing a piece with the band. This class may be repeated.

Discover the ukulele! Students who take this course will learn the fundamentals of playing ukulele, and reading ukulele chord charts and notation. From folk to funk, we will explore a variety of music through playing ukulele, working towards a recital at the end of the semester. Advanced ukulele students may also work towards accompanying the chorus. This class may be repeated.

courses.course_name: Cold Hollow Career Center: Pre-Technical Studies
courses.description: Pre Technical Studies is designed to provide 10th-grade students (9th graders may be accepted if space provides) with a unique experience in career exploration as they learn about and experience each of the various career development programs at CHCC. Throughout the first portion of the year, students work collaboratively to solve real-world problems related to each program in the center. They get hands-on experience in each program, learn about the various career opportunities related to each cluster, and visit local employers to see for themselves where professionals in these fields work and what work looks like on a daily basis. Later in the program, students are tasked with developing, executing, and reflecting upon an independently-designed career-based project that will further their learning and skills in a career that inspires them most. Throughout this course, students will have access to a variety of resources to build skills in the career of their choice. In addition to these tools and equipment, students may also have the opportunity to work with individual program instructors to help facilitate their learning. This program can assist in student preparation for 11th and 12th-grade technical programming as well as an insight into the world of work that awaits them as they approach adulthood. Program Highlights: ● Earn English, Math, Science, .5 PE, and .5 Art ● Investigation of all CHCC programs ● In-depth career pathway development ● A hands-on approach to learning ● Industry recognized credentials in First Aid and CPR Eligibility: Students in grade 10

courses.description: Driver education is offered to students who have obtained a valid driver’s permit. The class is offered after school once during the first semester, and again during the second semester. Students must sign up in the guidance office. A student who is 16 or 17 years old has to pass driver education in order to obtain a driver’s license in Vermont. Enrollment in Driver Education is based on the birth date of seniors and juniors, with this group having first priority. Sophomores are given next priority based on the student who had held his/her learner’s permit the longest. Freshmen are assigned on a space available basis, also based on the student who has held his/her learner’s permit the longest. In addition, if there are more students who have signed up than the allowed number in class, consideration may also be based upon academic performance, attendance, and behavioral data. This course consists of 30 hours of classroom instruction, six hours of behind-the-wheel driving and six hours of observation. Driving includes completion of the Partnership Driving Guide with the parent which requires 25 hours of practice at home with 5 of the hours being nighttime. Classroom topics include: knowledge of the rules of the road and driver responsibilities, basic vehicle control and maneuvers, managing risk, natural laws, drowsy driving, road rage, distracted driving, insurance and steps to follow in a crash, sharing the road with tractor trailers and motorcycles, driving in urban and rural areas, adverse driving conditions, alcohol and other drugs, buying and maintaining a vehicle and finding your way with use of maps, internet and GPS. Students will only receive a State of Vermont Certificate if they have completed all the required assigned work and have successfully passed the classroom and driving phase of the course.
courses.notes: Offered after school once during the first semester and again during the second semester; must have a valid driver's permit; sign up in the guidance office

courses.description: A required course for seniors, this will introduce values, goals and decision-making. A variety of case studies will be used to explore and become aware of the influences on life. Students will do a job unit where they will prepare a resume, application, and a cover letter for a specific job. Students will then conduct a mock interview with a written evaluation. Students will become aware of the different effects of deductions in a payroll unit. Students will be using a text book and worksheet material to identify the types of deductions by filing a W-4 form. Using information from case studies and information from the IRS, students will be able to file a 1040EZ tax form. Students will be introduced to various aspects of banking ending with a checkbook case study to cover a month’s worth of transactions. Students will be introduced to budgeting techniques and set up a budget using case studies.

VTVLC offers online courses taught by certified Vermont teachers. There are many reasons why students may take a VTVLC course: to minimize scheduling conflicts, to offer variety in their schedule (i.e. if VTVLC offers a course we do not), for enrichment purposes, or perhaps for credit recovery. Every effort will be made to schedule students’ VTVLC courses during the regular school day. If this is not possible, students will be responsible for working on their VTVLC course on their own time. Please note that students may not replace a RJSHS class that they can access in their regular schedule with a VTVLC course. VTVLC courses are intended to provide variety and flexibility. Enrolling in a VTVLC course requires prior approval from the Director of Guidance. See attached VTVLC catalog for an idea of what they offer.
courses.notes: program

courses.description: All Vermont high school students may enroll in two (2) free college courses by the time they graduate from high school by using a voucher. Students are responsible for any fees or text books associated with the college class. If students qualify, they may receive a $150 stipend from VSAC to help pay for course expenses. At this time, students may take college courses on any VT college campus (with the exception of Middlebury) or online (if the institution offers an online option). RJSHS also offers Dual Enrollment options that are built into the high school schedule and that are taught by Richford teachers (these are called Dual Enrollment Concurrent classes). Students may use their voucher for Concurrent Classes, or they may pay at a reduced rate of $150 per course. RJSHS will offer one (1) credit for successful completion of a college course (college transcript must be submitted to the guidance office). The grade and credit will be issued on the high school transcript, and will be averaged into the high school GPA and class rank. Students must meet with the Director of Guidance prior to enrolling in the college class to make sure that the class is a good fit, and to complete the necessary paperwork/contract.
courses.notes: program

courses.description: Students may complete their senior year of high school and first year of college simultaneously-tuition free. Students who are interested in this opportunity should meet with the Guidance Director and be prepared to apply during their junior year.
courses.notes: program

courses.description: Students may enroll as a Flexible Pathway Academy (FPA) student if they need or want a flexible option for high school. FPA can include online courses, in-person courses, project based learning, work based learning, or a combination of all these options. Students may elect to graduate with a traditional high school transcript (also known as a legacy transcript), or a Mastery Based transcript. A Mastery Based transcript measures skill acquisition versus credit completion. It is advised that you have a discussion with the Flexible Pathways Coordinator to determine which transcript is most appropriate for you.
courses.notes: program

courses.description: Students may gain knowledge and experience related to career development through opportunities such as: worksite visits and tours, career fairs, informational interviewing, job shadowing, unpaid/paid work experience, internships, and service learning. The purpose of WBL is for students to see the relevance between what they are learning in the classroom and real-world application. Additionally, students develop and refine important soft and technical skills necessary to be successful in the workplace. When appropriate, students may earn credit or prove proficiency in certain subject areas. Students must meet with the Work Based Learning Coordinator to set goals and develop a WBL plan. All WBL experiences should be added to students’ Personalized Learning Plans.
courses.notes: program

courses.description: Extended Learning Opportunities acknowledge that learning happens across all aspects of a person’s life. At RHS, we want to connect the learning that happens in school to learning and enrichment that happens during other endeavors. We want our learners to recognize that transferable and content specific skills are those that “transfer” across all settings, subject to subject in school, school to hobbies, school to work, even from job to job. ELOs provide learners with opportunities to demonstrate proficiency in all RHS Transferable Skills, as well as content specific areas, including those that might not be addressed through a learner's individual course path. Extended Learning Opportunities may take any number of forms (e.g., involvement in sports, clubs, theater, part-time jobs, educational summer camps, MedQuest, Boys' State, Girls' State, Governor's Institutes of VT , volunteering, etc). Anything that demonstrates one’s learning and growth offers a possibility for gathering evidence to demonstrate proficiency in a transferable skill indicator or content area.
courses.notes: program
